subject: history
title: Elizabeth I: Settlement, Mary Stuart and the Armada
welcome_lead: From the 1559 Settlement to the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on Elizabeth I: Religious Settlement 1559, execution of Mary Queen of Scots 1587 and the Armada 1588.
final_note: You can evaluate Elizabethan stability and the threats it survived.

walkthroughs.body_html: Elizabeth accepted the title Supreme Governor (not Head, easing Catholic and female-rule scruples). The Act of Uniformity (1559) imposed the 1559 Prayer Book, splitting the difference between 1549 and 1552; the Royal Injunctions (1559) regulated worship. The Settlement frustrated both Puritans (Vestments Controversy from 1566; Admonition to the Parliament 1572) and Catholics.

Mary Stuart fled to England in 1568. The Northern Rebellion (1569) and Ridolfi Plot (1571) circled around her. The papal bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) excommunicated Elizabeth. The Throckmorton Plot (1583) and especially the Babington Plot (1586) implicated Mary; Walsingham produced the incriminating evidence. Mary was executed at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587.

Philip II's 'Enterprise of England' launched in May 1588 under Medina Sidonia. After skirmishes up the Channel, English fireships at Calais (night of 7 August) broke the crescent formation, and at Gravelines (8 August) superior English gunnery prevailed. Storms scattered the fleet around Scotland and Ireland; perhaps 60 ships and over 10,000 men were lost. War with Spain dragged on until 1604.

options: Supreme Governor of the Church of England
Supreme Head of the Church
Defender of the Faith
Vicar of Christ in England

options: Babington Plot
Ridolfi Plot
Throckmorton Plot
Gunpowder Plot

mcqs.q: Why was the Spanish Armada defeated in 1588?
options: William of Orange was Charles II's son and inherited the throne.
Elizabeth I personally commanded the English fleet at sea.
Drake defeated the Armada single-handedly in a great sea battle.
A combination of English tactics and fireships, poor Spanish planning, and the 'Protestant wind' storms that wrecked the fleet on the return.

mcqs.q: Why is 1688 called the Glorious Revolution?
options: It was glorious because no one died anywhere in the conflict.
William of Orange was Charles II's son and inherited the throne.
Parliament invited William of Orange to replace the Catholic James II, with little bloodshed in England, establishing parliamentary supremacy and the 1689 Bill of Rights.
Elizabeth I personally commanded the English fleet at sea.

mcqs.q: What was the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559?
options: Elizabeth made England fully Protestant and banned Catholic worship outright.
Elizabeth I personally commanded the English fleet at sea.
Elizabeth reunited England with the Pope to make peace with Spain.
A deliberate via media — a Protestant doctrine and English-language prayer book combined with some Catholic-style ceremony — designed to maximise conformity.
